records.source: Πᾶς ὁ πιστεύων ὅτι Ἰησοῦς ἐστιν ὁ χριστὸς ἐκ τοῦ θεοῦ γεγέννηται, καὶ πᾶς ὁ ἀγαπῶν τὸν γεννήσαντα ἀγαπᾷ καὶ τὸν γεγεννημένον ἐξ αὐτοῦ.
records.gloss: Everyone the believing that Jesus is the Christ from the God has been born, and everyone the loving the [one] having fathered loves also the [one] having been fathered from him.
pieces: Everyone who believes that Jesus is the {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} has been born of God, and everyone who loves the Father loves the child born of {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} as well.

L.1: Everyone who believes that Jesus is the {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} has been born of God, and everyone who loves the one who fathered loves also the one fathered by {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}.

R.1: Everyone who believes that Jesus is the {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} has been born as a child of God. And everyone who loves God the Father also loves {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} children.

decisions.choice: believing that Jesus is the Christ goes together with having been born of God
alternatives: the new birth comes first and produces belief
decisions.reason: The verb for being born (γεγέννηται) is perfect: the birth is a settled fact, while the believing is present and ongoing. The sentence says that everyone who believes is born of God; it does not spell out which comes first. The same pairing of a present action with the perfect "has been born" is used of doing right (2:29) and loving (4:7).

decisions.choice: the Christ: the Messiah, God's anointed king
decisions.reason: With the article, ὁ χριστὸς is a title, as in 2:22: the confession is that the man Jesus is the promised Messiah. The christos setting gives "Christ" or "Messiah".

decisions.choice: a rule from family life applied to God and his children: whoever loves the parent loves the parent's child
alternatives: the one born of him is Jesus, the Son
a general proverb with no particular parent in view
decisions.reason: The one who fathered is God, named in the first half of the verse. The one born of him is any believer: the next verse speaks of "the children of God", and the first half of this verse has just said believers are born of God. The singular states a general rule that holds for each child. The other reading, that the child is Jesus, is possible, but the letter does not use this verb of the Son until 5:18.

decisions.choice: the Father
decisions.reason: The participle names God by what he did: he fathered the children. Balanced says "the Father", which is what the participle means here; Literal keeps the participle.

decisions.choice: has been born as a child of God; God the Father ... his children
alternatives: has been born of God; the one who fathered ... the one born of him
decisions.reason: Readable says what the birth makes a person (a child of God) and names God as the Father. It puts the rule in the plural, "his children", because the singular child stands for every believer (meaning decision m3).

records.heading: Born of God, overcoming the world

records.source: ἐν τούτῳ γινώσκομεν ὅτι ἀγαπῶμεν τὰ τέκνα τοῦ θεοῦ, ὅταν τὸν θεὸν ἀγαπῶμεν καὶ τὰς ἐντολὰς αὐτοῦ ποιῶμεν·
records.gloss: In this we know that we love the children of the God, whenever the God we love and the commandments of him we do;
pieces: We can tell that we love God's children when we love God and do what {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} commands.

L.2: In this we know that we love the children of God: whenever we love God and do {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} commandments;

R.2: We know that we love God's children when we love God and obey {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} commands.

decisions.choice: "in this" points forward to the "whenever" clause
decisions.reason: In 1 John ἐν τούτῳ can point either way; here the clause with ὅταν (whenever) supplies what "this" is.

decisions.choice: love for God and love for God's children cannot be separated, and each is a test of the other
alternatives: love for God depends on loving others first
decisions.reason: In 4:20 love for the brother or sister is the test of love for God; here love for God and obedience to him are the test of love for his children. The two verses look at the same bond from opposite sides; neither kind of love can exist without the other.

decisions.choice: God's children, of either sex
decisions.reason: τέκνα is neuter and already inclusive, so the gender setting does not apply.

decisions.choice: "do" his commandments (SBLGNT)
decisions.reason: Many later manuscripts have "keep", the verb John uses for commandments elsewhere in the letter and in the next verse; the SBLGNT follows manuscripts that read "do", the less usual expression. The meaning is the same, so no footnote. A reviewer should check this against the SBLGNT apparatus.

decisions.choice: do what he commands (B); obey his commands (R)
decisions.reason: "Do commandments" is not natural English; the sense is carrying them out. Literal keeps "do", the Greek verb.

records.source: αὕτη γάρ ἐστιν ἡ ἀγάπη τοῦ θεοῦ ἵνα τὰς ἐντολὰς αὐτοῦ τηρῶμεν, καὶ αἱ ἐντολαὶ αὐτοῦ βαρεῖαι οὐκ εἰσίν, ὅτι πᾶν τὸ γεγεννημένον ἐκ τοῦ θεοῦ νικᾷ τὸν κόσμον.
records.gloss: This for is the love of the God, that the commandments of him we keep, and the commandments of him heavy not are, \v 4 because everything the having been born from the God overcomes the world.
pieces: For to love God is to keep {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} commandments, and {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} commandments are no burden,
because everything born of God overcomes the world.

L.3: For this is the love of God, that we keep {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} commandments; and {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} commandments are not heavy,
L.4: because everything that has been born of God overcomes the world.

R.3: Loving God means obeying {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} commands. And {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} commands are not too hard for us,
R.4: because every child of God overcomes the world.

decisions.choice: love for God
decisions.reason: The genitive could name God as the one who loves or as the one loved. Verse 2 has just spoken of loving God, and the love is shown in keeping his commandments, so it is our love for him.

decisions.choice: not burdensome, not a crushing weight
decisions.reason: βαρεῖαι means heavy, and so oppressive (compare the heavy burdens of Matthew 23:4). The point is not that obeying costs nothing but that the commandments do not crush the one who is born of God, because that person has the strength to overcome. Compare Deuteronomy 30:11, where God's commandment is not too hard or far away.

decisions.choice: everything born of God: every person born of God, put as a whole
alternatives: only certain things given by God
decisions.reason: The neuter πᾶν τὸ γεγεννημένον speaks of all who are born of God as one whole (compare John 6:37, 39, where the neuter "all that" also stands for people). It means believers, as 5:1 and 5:4b show.

decisions.choice: the world: human life organized apart from God and against him
decisions.reason: Key term. As in 2:15-17 and 4:4-5, the world is the realm that does not know God and is under the evil one (5:19). To overcome it is to stand firm against it, as Jesus overcame the world (John 16:33).

decisions.choice: to love God is to keep his commandments
alternatives: this is the love of God, that we keep his commandments
decisions.reason: Balanced states the equation plainly, using the sense in meaning decision m1; "the love of God" could be read as God's love for us.

decisions.choice: every child of God
decisions.reason: Readable names the people meant (meaning decision m3) in the wording 5:1 uses.

records.source: καὶ αὕτη ἐστὶν ἡ νίκη ἡ νικήσασα τὸν κόσμον, ἡ πίστις ἡμῶν·
records.gloss: And this is the victory the having overcome the world, the faith of us;
pieces: And our faith is the victory that overcame the world.

L.4: And this is the victory that overcame the world: our faith;

R.4: Our faith is how we have won the victory over the world.

decisions.choice: the victory that overcame: a victory already won
alternatives: a victory that keeps on being won
decisions.reason: The participle νικήσασα is aorist, unlike the present "overcomes" just before. It looks back to a victory already won: the moment believers came to faith, which shares in Jesus' own victory (John 16:33 "I have overcome the world"; compare 1 John 2:13-14; 4:4).

decisions.choice: our faith: our believing that Jesus is the Son of God
decisions.reason: Key term. This is the only place the noun πίστις occurs in John's letters, and John's Gospel never uses it; elsewhere John always uses the verb "believe". The next verse defines it: believing that Jesus is the Son of God.

decisions.choice: our faith first
alternatives: this is the victory that overcame the world: our faith
decisions.reason: The Greek puts "our faith" last for emphasis. Balanced and Readable make it the subject, which keeps the weight on it without the delayed construction.

decisions.choice: how we have won the victory over the world
alternatives: the victory that overcame the world
decisions.reason: Readable says what the faith does in plain words; the other levels keep "overcame" so the verb links to verses 4a and 5.

records.source: τίς δέ ἐστιν ὁ νικῶν τὸν κόσμον εἰ μὴ ὁ πιστεύων ὅτι Ἰησοῦς ἐστιν ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ θεοῦ;
records.gloss: Who and is the [one] overcoming the world if not the [one] believing that Jesus is the Son of the God?
pieces: Who overcomes the world, if not the one who believes that Jesus is the Son of God?

L.5: And who is the one who overcomes the world, if not the one who believes that Jesus is the Son of God?

R.5: Who wins the victory over the world? No one but the person who believes that Jesus is the Son of God.

decisions.choice: a question that expects the answer: only the believer
decisions.reason: The question with "if not" is a strong way of saying that the believer, and no one else, overcomes the world. It names the faith of 5:4b: believing that Jesus is the Son of God.

decisions.choice: Jesus himself is the Son of God
alternatives: the Son of God is a being distinct from the man Jesus
decisions.reason: The confession is that the man Jesus is the Son of God, not merely that a heavenly Son exists. 4:2-3 and 5:6 press the same point against those who left the community (2:19).

decisions.choice: a question and a separate answer
decisions.reason: Readable turns the rhetorical question into a question and its answer, which is what the Greek means (meaning decision m1).

records.source: Οὗτός ἐστιν ὁ ἐλθὼν δι’ ὕδατος καὶ αἵματος, Ἰησοῦς Χριστός· οὐκ ἐν τῷ ὕδατι μόνον ἀλλ’ ἐν τῷ ὕδατι καὶ ἐν τῷ αἵματι· καὶ τὸ πνεῦμά ἐστιν τὸ μαρτυροῦν, ὅτι τὸ πνεῦμά ἐστιν ἡ ἀλήθεια.
records.gloss: This is the [one] having come through water and blood, Jesus Christ; not in the water only but in the water and in the blood; and the Spirit is the [one] testifying, because the Spirit is the truth.
pieces: This is the one who came by water and blood: Jesus {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}. He came not with the water only, but with the water and with the blood. And it is the Spirit who testifies, because the Spirit is the truth.

L.6: This is the one who came through water and blood, Jesus {{christos:Christ|Messiah}}; not in the water only, but in the water and in the blood; and the Spirit is the one who testifies, because the Spirit is the truth.

R.6: Jesus {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} is the one who came through water and blood. He did not come with the water only. He came with the water and with the blood. And the Spirit is a witness to this, because the Spirit is the truth.

decisions.choice: water and blood: most likely Jesus' baptism and his death on the cross
alternatives: the water and blood that flowed from Jesus' side when he died (John 19:34)
the sacraments of baptism and the Lord's Supper
decisions.reason: "Came" is aorist and looks at Jesus' coming in the past, so water and blood are events in his life. The most likely reading is his baptism, where the Spirit came on him and he was made known (John 1:31-34), and his death, where his blood was shed (1:7). "Not in the water only" seems aimed at teachers who accepted the baptism but denied that the Christ died; the letter insists that Jesus Christ came in the flesh (4:2). The other side: John 19:34-35 also joins water, blood and witness at the cross, and the writer may have that moment in mind. The text does not say which events it means, so a footnote gives the other readings.

decisions.choice: through ... in: two ways of saying the same coming
alternatives: a different meaning for each preposition
decisions.reason: The first phrase uses δι (through), the second ἐν (in, with). Both describe the means and circumstances of his coming; the change does not mark a different idea.

decisions.choice: because the Spirit is the truth
alternatives: that the Spirit is the truth (what the Spirit testifies)
decisions.reason: ὅτι could give the reason (because) or the content (testifies that). The Spirit's witness is trustworthy because the Spirit is the truth itself (John 14:17; 15:26, "the Spirit of truth"); the content of his testimony is about the Son (5:9-11), not about himself.

decisions.choice: water and blood (SBLGNT)
alternatives: water and blood and Spirit (some manuscripts)
decisions.reason: Some manuscripts add "and Spirit" or "and Holy Spirit" after "blood", or replace "blood" with "Spirit", probably under the influence of John 3:5 and of verse 8. The SBLGNT follows manuscripts with the shorter text. A reviewer should check this against the SBLGNT apparatus.

decisions.choice: with the water ... with the blood
alternatives: in the water ... in the blood
decisions.reason: English "in the water" suggests standing in water. "With" carries the sense of meaning decision m2; Literal keeps "in".

decisions.choice: is a witness to this
decisions.reason: Readable uses the plainer "witness" and says what the Spirit testifies to: Jesus' coming just described.

records.source: ὅτι τρεῖς εἰσιν οἱ μαρτυροῦντες, τὸ πνεῦμα καὶ τὸ ὕδωρ καὶ τὸ αἷμα, καὶ οἱ τρεῖς εἰς τὸ ἕν εἰσιν.
records.gloss: Because three are the [ones] testifying, \v 8 the Spirit and the water and the blood, and the three into the one are.
pieces: For there are three that testify:
the Spirit, the water and the blood, and the three are in agreement.

L.7: For there are three who testify,
L.8: the Spirit and the water and the blood, and the three are for the one [thing].

R.8: the Spirit, the water and the blood. And all three say the same thing.

decisions.choice: the short text, as in the SBLGNT: three that testify, the Spirit, the water and the blood
alternatives: the long text known as the Johannine Comma, which adds in verse 7 "in heaven, the Father, the Word and the Holy Spirit, and these three are one" and in verse 8 "there are three that testify on earth"
decisions.reason: The longer wording is not found in any Greek manuscript before the late medieval period; it appears in only a handful of late Greek manuscripts, some of them with the words added in the margin by a later hand. No Greek writer of the early church quotes it, even in the fourth-century debates about the Trinity, where it would have been the most useful verse to cite. It first appears in Latin writers and then in later copies of the Latin Bible, and it is missing from the oldest Latin Bible manuscripts and from the early translations into other languages. It probably began as a comment explaining the three witnesses, which was later copied into the text. From the Latin tradition it entered the printed Greek New Testament in the sixteenth century, and so the Textus Receptus and the King James Version (1611). The SBLGNT does not print it, and no level of this translation includes it. The doctrine of the Trinity does not rest on this passage. A reviewer must check this account against the SBLGNT apparatus and the manuscript evidence before the sentence is marked meaning reviewed.

decisions.choice: for: it explains the Spirit's testimony in verse 6
decisions.reason: ὅτι links the verse to the end of verse 6: the Spirit testifies, and it does not testify alone. Under the law of Moses a matter is settled by two or three witnesses (Deuteronomy 19:15; compare John 8:17).

decisions.choice: the three agree: they point to one and the same truth
decisions.reason: εἰς τὸ ἕν εἰσιν means literally "are into the one", that is, they converge on one thing: the single testimony about the Son (5:9-11). It says they agree, not that they are the same.

decisions.choice: the Spirit, the water and the blood: the Spirit's present witness together with the events of Jesus' baptism and death
alternatives: three sacraments or rites in the church's life
decisions.reason: The water and the blood are those of verse 6. The verbs are now present ("there are three that testify"): what happened at Jesus' baptism and death still bears witness, together with the Spirit. Some see a reference to baptism and the Lord's Supper in the church; the text does not say so.

decisions.choice: all three say the same thing
decisions.reason: Readable puts the idiom (meaning decision m3) in everyday words.

decisions.choice: So
decisions.reason: Readable uses "So" to start a fresh sentence that still follows on from verse 6; "For" at the start of a sentence is formal.

records.source: εἰ τὴν μαρτυρίαν τῶν ἀνθρώπων λαμβάνομεν, ἡ μαρτυρία τοῦ θεοῦ μείζων ἐστίν, ὅτι αὕτη ἐστὶν ἡ μαρτυρία τοῦ θεοῦ ὅτι μεμαρτύρηκεν περὶ τοῦ υἱοῦ αὐτοῦ.
records.gloss: If the testimony of the human beings we receive, the testimony of the God greater is, because this is the testimony of the God, that he has testified about the Son of him.
pieces: We accept the testimony of {{gender:people|men}}; the testimony of God is greater, for this is the testimony God has given: {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} has testified about {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} Son.

L.9: If we receive the testimony of {{gender:human beings|men}}, the testimony of God is greater, because this is the testimony of God, that {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} has testified about {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} Son.

R.9: We believe what {{gender:people|men}} tell us when they are witnesses. But what God tells us is far more important. And God has told us about {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} Son.

decisions.choice: if, as we do: a condition assumed to be true
alternatives: if, as may or may not be the case
decisions.reason: The condition states a fact: people do accept human witnesses, as the law requires (Deuteronomy 19:15). The argument goes from the lesser to the greater.

decisions.choice: this is God's testimony: that he has testified about his Son
alternatives: because he has testified about his Son
decisions.reason: The first ὅτι gives the reason God's testimony applies here; the second (ὅτι) states what the testimony is. The perfect μεμαρτύρηκεν means his testimony was given and still stands. It is the witness of verses 6-8, and verses 10-11 say what it contains.

decisions.choice: human beings, men and women
decisions.reason: The plural is general, so the gender setting applies.

decisions.choice: that he has testified (SBLGNT)
alternatives: which he has testified (many later manuscripts)
decisions.reason: Many later manuscripts, followed by the Textus Receptus, read a relative pronoun ("which he has testified") in place of ὅτι. The sense is close, so no footnote. A reviewer should check this against the SBLGNT apparatus.

decisions.choice: no "if": We accept ...
decisions.reason: English "if" suggests doubt; Balanced states the fact the condition assumes (meaning decision m1). Literal keeps "if".

decisions.choice: what people tell us when they are witnesses ... far more important
decisions.reason: Readable explains "testimony" as what a witness tells and "greater" as more important and more trustworthy. It leaves out the explanatory "this is God's testimony" and says what it is.

records.source: ὁ πιστεύων εἰς τὸν υἱὸν τοῦ θεοῦ ἔχει τὴν μαρτυρίαν ἐν αὑτῷ· ὁ μὴ πιστεύων τῷ θεῷ ψεύστην πεποίηκεν αὐτόν, ὅτι οὐ πεπίστευκεν εἰς τὴν μαρτυρίαν ἣν μεμαρτύρηκεν ὁ θεὸς περὶ τοῦ υἱοῦ αὐτοῦ.
records.gloss: The [one] believing into the Son of the God has the testimony in himself; the [one] not believing the God a liar has made him, because not he has believed into the testimony which has testified the God about the Son of him.
pieces: Whoever believes in the Son of God has this testimony within. Whoever does not believe God has made {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} a liar, by refusing to believe the testimony God has given about {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} Son.

L.10: The one who believes in the Son of God has the testimony in {{gender:themselves|himself}}; the one who does not believe God has made {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} a liar, because {{gender:they have|he has}} not believed in the testimony that God has testified about {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} Son.

R.10: If you believe in the Son of God, you have God's testimony in your own heart. If you do not believe God, you are calling {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} a liar. You have not believed what God has said about {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} Son.

decisions.choice: in himself: the believer has God's testimony within
alternatives: in him, that is, in the Son
decisions.reason: The SBLGNT reads αὑτῷ with a rough breathing, the reflexive "himself": the one who believes has taken God's testimony inside, where it remains (compare 2:14, 24). Some manuscripts read "in him", which could refer to the Son. A reviewer should check the breathing and the variant against the SBLGNT apparatus.

decisions.choice: believe in the Son; believe God; believe in the testimony
decisions.reason: John uses "believe in" for trusting a person (the Son) and "believe" with a plain object for accepting what someone says (God). The last clause unusually says "believed in the testimony": not accepting what God says is refusing to trust him.

decisions.choice: to reject God's testimony is to call God a liar
decisions.reason: God has given his word about his Son; refusing it treats him as one who lies, as 1:10 says of those who deny they have sinned.

decisions.choice: does not believe God (SBLGNT)
alternatives: does not believe the Son (some manuscripts)
decisions.reason: Some manuscripts read "the Son" in place of "God", in line with the first half of the verse. A reviewer should check this against the SBLGNT apparatus.

decisions.choice: whoever (B); if you (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced uses the general "whoever" and avoids a pronoun for the believer; Readable speaks to the reader directly, which keeps the general sense in plain words.

decisions.choice: in your own heart
decisions.reason: Readable says where the testimony is kept, using the ordinary image for the inner person.

records.source: καὶ αὕτη ἐστὶν ἡ μαρτυρία, ὅτι ζωὴν αἰώνιον ἔδωκεν ὁ θεὸς ἡμῖν, καὶ αὕτη ἡ ζωὴ ἐν τῷ υἱῷ αὐτοῦ ἐστιν.
records.gloss: And this is the testimony, that life eternal gave the God to us, and this the life in the Son of him is.
pieces: And here is what the testimony says: God gave us eternal life, and that life is found in {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} Son.

L.11: And this is the testimony: that eternal life God gave to us, and this life is in {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} Son.

R.11: This is what God's testimony says: God has given us eternal life, and this life is found in {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} Son.

decisions.choice: eternal life: the life of God himself, given now and lasting forever
alternatives: life that only begins after death
decisions.reason: Key term. In John's writings eternal life is the life that was with the Father and appeared in Jesus (1:2), given to believers now (5:12-13; John 5:24) and never ending.

decisions.choice: God gave: a gift given once, which believers now have
decisions.reason: The aorist ἔδωκεν looks at the giving as a completed act; verse 12 says the believer now has the life.

decisions.choice: the life is in the Son: it is had only by having him
decisions.reason: The life is not a thing God hands over apart from the Son; it is in him, so to have the Son is to have the life (verse 12; John 1:4; 14:6).

decisions.choice: is found in
decisions.reason: "Found" makes clear that the Son is where the life is (meaning decision m3); Literal keeps "is in".

records.source: ὁ ἔχων τὸν υἱὸν ἔχει τὴν ζωήν· ὁ μὴ ἔχων τὸν υἱὸν τοῦ θεοῦ τὴν ζωὴν οὐκ ἔχει.
records.gloss: The [one] having the Son has the life; the [one] not having the Son of the God the life not has.
pieces: Anyone who has the Son has the life; anyone without the Son of God does not have the life.

L.12: The one who has the Son has the life; the one who does not have the Son of God does not have the life.

R.12: People who have the Son have this life. People who do not have the Son of God do not have this life.

decisions.choice: the life: the eternal life just named in verse 11
decisions.reason: Both times the noun has the article, which points back to "this life" in verse 11.

decisions.choice: to have the Son: to belong to him by believing in him
alternatives: to know facts about the Son
decisions.reason: "Having" the Son, as in 2:23 ("having the Father") and 2 John 9, means being joined to him in a living relationship, which comes by believing (verses 10 and 13).

decisions.choice: the life (L, B); this life (R)
decisions.reason: The article is kept so that the reader hears that the life meant is the eternal life of verse 11 (meaning decision m1).

records.source: Ταῦτα ἔγραψα ὑμῖν ἵνα εἰδῆτε ὅτι ζωὴν ἔχετε αἰώνιον, τοῖς πιστεύουσιν εἰς τὸ ὄνομα τοῦ υἱοῦ τοῦ θεοῦ.
records.gloss: These things I wrote to you so that you may know that life you have eternal, to the [ones] believing into the name of the Son of the God.
pieces: I have written these things to you so that you may know that you have eternal life—you who believe in the name of the Son of God.

L.13: These things I wrote to you so that you may know that you have life eternal, to you who believe in the name of the Son of God.

R.13: You believe in the Son of God. I have written this letter to you so that you can know for sure that you have eternal life.

decisions.choice: these things I have written: the letter as a whole, and especially 5:1-12
decisions.reason: ἔγραψα is an aorist written from the reader's point of view: by the time they read it, the writing is done. "These things" naturally takes in the letter and sums up its purpose, though it follows closely on 5:1-12.

decisions.choice: an echo of John 20:31
decisions.reason: John's Gospel states its purpose in similar words: written so that you may believe and have life in his name. The letter is written to those who already believe, so that they may know they have that life.

decisions.choice: believe in the name: believe in the person
decisions.reason: In Hebrew thought a name stands for the person (as in John 1:12).

decisions.choice: the short text (SBLGNT)
alternatives: a longer text in many later manuscripts and the Textus Receptus, which places "to you who believe in the name of the Son of God" earlier and adds at the end "and so that you may believe in the name of the Son of God"
decisions.reason: The longer wording, found in the King James Version, repeats the phrase about believing in the name and appears to expand the sentence. The SBLGNT follows earlier manuscripts with the shorter text. A reviewer should check this against the SBLGNT apparatus.

decisions.choice: the phrase about believers placed last, after a dash
alternatives: to you who believe ... placed first
decisions.reason: The Greek adds "to the ones who believe" at the end; Balanced keeps it there.

decisions.choice: this letter; know for sure
decisions.reason: Readable says what "these things" are (meaning decision m1) and uses "know for sure" for a verb that means knowing with certainty, which is the point of the sentence. It puts the description of the readers first, as its own sentence.

records.heading: Knowing we have eternal life

records.source: καὶ αὕτη ἐστὶν ἡ παρρησία ἣν ἔχομεν πρὸς αὐτόν, ὅτι ἐάν τι αἰτώμεθα κατὰ τὸ θέλημα αὐτοῦ ἀκούει ἡμῶν.
records.gloss: And this is the boldness which we have toward him, that if anything we ask according to the will of him he hears us.
pieces: And here is the boldness we have in coming to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}: whenever we ask for something in line with {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} will, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} listens to us.

L.14: And this is the boldness that we have toward {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}: that if we ask something according to {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} will, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} hears us.

R.14: We can come to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} without fear. If we ask for anything that {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} wants, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} listens to us.

decisions.choice: boldness, freedom to speak openly
decisions.reason: παρρησία is the freedom to speak plainly and without fear, here before God. In 2:28 and 4:17 it is the boldness of believers on the day of judgment; in 3:21-22 and here it is boldness in prayer.

decisions.choice: him: God, to whom prayer is made
alternatives: the Son of God, named in verse 13
decisions.reason: In 3:21-22 the same boldness in asking is "before God", and asking according to "his will" fits God the Father. The pronoun could also refer to the Son, the last person named, and in John 14:14 Jesus speaks of being asked in his name. The levels keep the pronoun.

decisions.choice: asking in line with God's will is the condition, not a limit on God's hearing
decisions.reason: The sentence does not promise that any request will be granted, but that God hears every request made in keeping with his will. 3:22 adds keeping his commandments and doing what pleases him.

decisions.choice: hears us: listens with favor
decisions.reason: As in John 9:31 and 11:41-42, God's hearing means he attends to the request and grants it; verse 15 says so.

decisions.choice: listens to us
decisions.reason: "Listens" carries the sense of meaning decision m4 better than "hears", which can mean only that sound reaches the ear. Literal keeps "hears".

decisions.choice: We can come to him without fear
alternatives: this is the boldness we have toward him
decisions.reason: Readable explains "boldness" (meaning decision m1) as approaching God without fear.

records.source: καὶ ἐὰν οἴδαμεν ὅτι ἀκούει ἡμῶν ὃ ἐὰν αἰτώμεθα, οἴδαμεν ὅτι ἔχομεν τὰ αἰτήματα ἃ ᾐτήκαμεν ἀπ’ αὐτοῦ.
records.gloss: And if we know that he hears us whatever we ask, we know that we have the requests which we have asked from him.
pieces: And if we know that {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} hears us in whatever we ask, we know that the requests we have made of {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} are ours.

L.15: And if we know that {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} hears us, whatever we ask, we know that we have the requests that we have asked from {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}.

R.15: Since we know {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} listens to us whenever we ask, we also know that what we asked {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} for is ours.

decisions.choice: if, as is the case: since we know
decisions.reason: ἐὰν usually takes a subjunctive; here it takes the indicative οἴδαμεν, so it works like "if" stating a fact: since we know.

decisions.choice: we have the requests: they are already ours, though not yet seen
alternatives: we will receive the requests later
decisions.reason: The present ἔχομεν says that what was asked is already possessed; the answer is certain, even if it comes later.

decisions.choice: Since
decisions.reason: Readable states the fact the condition assumes (meaning decision m1).

records.source: ἐάν τις ἴδῃ τὸν ἀδελφὸν αὐτοῦ ἁμαρτάνοντα ἁμαρτίαν μὴ πρὸς θάνατον, αἰτήσει, καὶ δώσει αὐτῷ ζωήν, τοῖς ἁμαρτάνουσιν μὴ πρὸς θάνατον.
records.gloss: If anyone sees the brother of him sinning a sin not toward death, he will ask, and he will give to him life, to the [ones] sinning not toward death.
pieces: If anyone sees {{gender:their brother or sister|his brother}} committing a sin that does not lead to death, {{gender:they|he}} should ask, and God will give that person life. This is for those whose sin does not lead to death.

L.16: If anyone sees {{gender:their brother or sister|his brother}} sinning a sin not to death, {{gender:they|he}} will ask, and [God] will give {{gender:them|him}} life, to those who sin not to death.

R.16: If anyone sees a fellow believer doing something sinful that does not lead to death, {{gender:they|he}} should pray for that believer, and God will give that person life. This is for people whose sin does not lead to death.

decisions.choice: sin not leading to death: sin that does not cut a person off from life
alternatives: sin that does not cause bodily death
decisions.reason: The phrase means, word for word, sin "toward death": sin that leads to death. The letter does not say what that sin is, whether the death is the loss of eternal life or bodily death, or how another believer would recognize it. In the letter, "life" is eternal life (5:11-13) and its opposite is remaining in death (3:14), so many take the sin leading to death as the refusal of Jesus that marks those who left the community (2:19, 22-23; 4:1-3; 5:10-12): rejecting the Son is rejecting the life that is in him. Others think of deliberate, persistent sin, as in the Old Testament contrast between unintentional sins and sins "with a high hand" (Numbers 15:27-31), or of sins that God punished with death (Acts 5:1-11; 1 Corinthians 11:30). The text does not settle the question, so a footnote names the readings.

decisions.choice: he will ask: a future that works as an instruction (he should ask)
decisions.reason: The future αἰτήσει, in the main clause after "if", here states what should happen, as futures often do in commands. The asking is the prayer of verses 14-15.

decisions.choice: God will give life to the one who sinned
alternatives: the one who prays will give him life (through the prayer)
decisions.reason: Grammatically the subject of δώσει is most naturally the same as that of "will ask": the one who prays. But life is God's gift (5:11), so the one who prays gives it only as the means through which God gives it. Either way, God is the source of the life and the sinner receives it; the levels name God as the giver.

decisions.choice: brother or sister: a fellow believer
decisions.reason: In 1 John ἀδελφός means a fellow member of the believing community, man or woman, so the gender setting applies (as in 2:9-11; 3:14-17; 4:20-21).

decisions.choice: {{gender:their brother or sister|his brother}} ... {{gender:they|he}} ... {{gender:them|him}}
decisions.reason: Inclusive default, traditional one tap away. Readable says "a fellow believer" and "that believer", which need no setting; only its pronoun for "anyone" takes one.

decisions.choice: [God] (L); God (B, R)
decisions.reason: The levels name the giver (meaning decision m3); Literal marks the word as supplied.

decisions.choice: pray for that believer
decisions.reason: "Ask" is the word for prayer in verses 14-15; Readable says "pray" so the young reader knows who is asked and for whom.

records.source: ἔστιν ἁμαρτία πρὸς θάνατον· οὐ περὶ ἐκείνης λέγω ἵνα ἐρωτήσῃ.
records.gloss: There is sin toward death; not about that [one] do I say that he should ask.
pieces: There is sin that leads to death. I am not saying that anyone should make request about that.

L.16: There is sin to death; I do not say that one should make request about that.

R.16: There is sin that leads to death. I am not telling you to pray about that kind of sin.

decisions.choice: sin leading to death: not defined in the text
alternatives: apostasy, refusing Jesus as the Christ
a sin punished by bodily death
decisions.reason: The phrase means, word for word, sin "toward death": sin that leads to death. The letter does not say what that sin is, whether the death is the loss of eternal life or bodily death, or how another believer would recognize it. In the letter, "life" is eternal life (5:11-13) and its opposite is remaining in death (3:14), so many take the sin leading to death as the refusal of Jesus that marks those who left the community (2:19, 22-23; 4:1-3; 5:10-12): rejecting the Son is rejecting the life that is in him. Others think of deliberate, persistent sin, as in the Old Testament contrast between unintentional sins and sins "with a high hand" (Numbers 15:27-31), or of sins that God punished with death (Acts 5:1-11; 1 Corinthians 11:30). The text does not settle the question, so a footnote names the readings.

decisions.choice: John does not command prayer for it; he does not forbid it
alternatives: prayer for such a person is forbidden
decisions.reason: The words are "I do not say that he should ask". The writer gives no instruction for this case; he does not say that such prayer is wrong. He also changes the verb, from αἰτήσει in the previous sentence to ἐρωτήσῃ, which may mean making a request on someone's behalf; the difference is not clear.

decisions.choice: sin, without the article: sin of a kind
decisions.reason: ἁμαρτία has no article: the sentence speaks of a kind of sinning, not of one named act.

decisions.choice: make request (L, B); pray (R)
decisions.reason: Literal and Balanced use a different word from "ask" in the previous sentence because the Greek changes the verb (meaning decision m2). Readable keeps "pray" as in the previous sentence.

decisions.choice: about that kind of sin
decisions.reason: Readable says what "that" refers to and keeps the sense that the text names a kind of sin (meaning decision m3).

records.source: πᾶσα ἀδικία ἁμαρτία ἐστίν, καὶ ἔστιν ἁμαρτία οὐ πρὸς θάνατον.
records.gloss: All wrongdoing sin is, and there is sin not toward death.
pieces: All wrongdoing is sin, and yet there is sin that does not lead to death.

L.17: All wrongdoing is sin, and there is sin not to death.

R.17: Every wrong thing we do is sin. But not all sin leads to death.

decisions.choice: wrongdoing: any act that is not right
decisions.reason: ἀδικία is the opposite of doing what is right (1:9); the sentence warns that no wrong is harmless, even though not every sin leads to death.

decisions.choice: and yet: the second clause balances the first
decisions.reason: The verse holds two things together: all wrongdoing is sin and must be taken seriously, and yet sin not leading to death can be prayed for and forgiven (verse 16).

decisions.choice: not all sin leads to death
alternatives: there is sin that does not lead to death
decisions.reason: Readable restates the second clause in a simpler form that says the same thing.

records.source: Οἴδαμεν ὅτι πᾶς ὁ γεγεννημένος ἐκ τοῦ θεοῦ οὐχ ἁμαρτάνει, ἀλλ’ ὁ γεννηθεὶς ἐκ τοῦ θεοῦ τηρεῖ αὐτόν, καὶ ὁ πονηρὸς οὐχ ἅπτεται αὐτοῦ.
records.gloss: We know that everyone the having been born from the God not sins, but the [one] having been born from the God keeps him, and the evil [one] not touches him.
pieces: We know that anyone born of God does not go on sinning; rather, the Son, who was born of God, keeps {{gender:them|him}} safe, and the evil one does not lay hold of {{gender:them|him}}.

L.18: We know that everyone who has been born of God does not sin, but the one who was born of God keeps {{gender:them|him}}, and the evil one does not touch {{gender:them|him}}.

R.18: We know that God's children do not keep on sinning. The Son of God keeps them safe, and the evil one does not get hold of them.

decisions.choice: does not go on sinning: does not live in sin
decisions.reason: The present ἁμαρτάνει describes a settled way of life, as in 3:6 and 3:9. The letter has already said that believers do sin and must confess it (1:8-2:2), and 5:16 has just spoken of a believer who sins.

decisions.choice: the one born of God who keeps is Jesus, the Son; he keeps the believer
decisions.reason: The first participle (γεγεννημένος) is perfect, as everywhere in the letter for believers. The second (γεννηθεὶς) is aorist and appears to mean someone else: the Son, who keeps those the Father gave him (John 17:12). The SBLGNT reads αὐτόν (him), the believer whom the Son keeps. Many manuscripts read the reflexive pronoun (ἑαυτοῦ, as in 5:21: "keeps himself"), so that the believer guards himself, as in 5:21, and that reading is followed by the King James Version. The letter nowhere else calls Jesus "born of God", which is the other side. A footnote gives the other reading.

decisions.choice: him (SBLGNT)
decisions.reason: Many manuscripts, including some early ones, read the reflexive "himself"; others read "him" as the SBLGNT does. The choice goes with meaning decision m2. A reviewer should check this against the SBLGNT apparatus.

decisions.choice: the evil one does not touch him: cannot seize or harm him
alternatives: does not come into contact with him at all
decisions.reason: ἅπτεται here means to lay hold of in order to harm. The evil one is the devil (2:13-14; 3:8, 12), who holds the whole world (5:19) but cannot get hold of the one the Son keeps.

decisions.choice: the Son, who was born of God (B); the Son of God (R)
alternatives: the one who was born of God
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name the one meant (meaning decision m2). Literal keeps the bare participle.

decisions.choice: God's children ... them
alternatives: everyone who has been born of God ... him
decisions.reason: Readable puts the general singular in the plural, which needs no gender setting.

decisions.choice: {{gender:them|him}}
decisions.reason: The pronoun stands for any believer, so the gender setting applies.

records.heading: What we know

records.source: οἴδαμεν ὅτι ἐκ τοῦ θεοῦ ἐσμεν, καὶ ὁ κόσμος ὅλος ἐν τῷ πονηρῷ κεῖται.
records.gloss: We know that from the God we are, and the world whole in the evil [one] lies.
pieces: We know that we belong to God, and that the whole world lies in the grip of the evil one.

L.19: We know that we are of God, and the whole world lies in the evil one.

R.19: We know that we belong to God. But the whole world is held in the power of the evil one.

decisions.choice: we are of God: we come from God and belong to him
alternatives: we are God's in origin only
decisions.reason: "Of God" (ἐκ τοῦ θεοῦ) in 1 John speaks of where a person comes from and to whom they belong (3:10; 4:4, 6); it echoes being born of God in verse 18.

decisions.choice: the evil one, a person
decisions.reason: The form can be masculine or neuter. Verse 18 has just named "the evil one", so it is the devil here too.

decisions.choice: the world: humanity organized apart from God
decisions.reason: Key term. As in 5:4, the world is not the creation as such but human life set against God.

decisions.choice: lies in the evil one: lies under his power, passive in his hands
decisions.reason: The verb means to lie, to be placed: the world lies passive in the evil one's hold.

decisions.choice: lies in the grip of (B); is held in the power of (R)
decisions.reason: "Lies in the evil one" is unclear in English; Balanced and Readable say what it means (meaning decision m4).

records.source: οἴδαμεν δὲ ὅτι ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ θεοῦ ἥκει, καὶ δέδωκεν ἡμῖν διάνοιαν ἵνα γινώσκωμεν τὸν ἀληθινόν· καὶ ἐσμὲν ἐν τῷ ἀληθινῷ, ἐν τῷ υἱῷ αὐτοῦ Ἰησοῦ Χριστῷ.
records.gloss: We know and that the Son of the God has come, and he has given to us understanding so that we may know the true [one]; and we are in the true [one], in the Son of him Jesus Christ.
pieces: We know too that the Son of God has come and has given us insight to know the one who is true. And we are in the one who is true, since we are in {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} Son, Jesus {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}.

L.20: And we know that the Son of God has come, and has given us understanding so that we may know the true one; and we are in the true one, in {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} Son Jesus {{christos:Christ|Messiah}}.

R.20: We also know that the Son of God has come. He has helped us understand, so that we know the true God. And we are joined to the true God because we are joined to {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} Son, Jesus {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}.

decisions.choice: has come: he came and is now here
decisions.reason: ἥκει is present in form but means "have come and be present".

decisions.choice: the true one: God the Father, the real God
alternatives: the one who tells the truth
decisions.reason: ἀληθινός means real, genuine, as opposed to false gods (verse 21; John 17:3, "the only true God"). The next words, "his Son", show that the true one here is the Father.

decisions.choice: we are in the true one by being in his Son
alternatives: two separate statements: we are in the Father, and we are in the Son
the true one is the Son
decisions.reason: The second "in" phrase explains the first: believers are in God because they are in his Son (2:23-24; John 14:6, 20; 17:21). Because the Son is "his Son", the true one cannot here be the Son himself.

decisions.choice: understanding: the ability to know and grasp
decisions.reason: διάνοιαν is the capacity to understand; the Son gives it so that believers know God himself.

decisions.choice: the true one (SBLGNT)
decisions.reason: Some manuscripts add "God" after "the true one". The sense is the same, so no footnote. A reviewer should check this against the SBLGNT apparatus.

decisions.choice: the true God
decisions.reason: Readable names the true one (meaning decision m2).

decisions.choice: since we are in (B); because we are joined to (R)
decisions.reason: The levels make explicit how the two "in" phrases are linked (meaning decision m3). Readable says "joined to" for being "in" someone, which young readers can picture.

records.source: οὗτός ἐστιν ὁ ἀληθινὸς θεὸς καὶ ζωὴ αἰώνιος.
records.gloss: This is the true God and life eternal.
pieces: This one is the true God, and eternal life.

L.20: This one is the true God and life eternal.

R.20: This one is the true God. This one is eternal life.

decisions.choice: "this one" may be Jesus Christ or God the Father; the text leaves it open
alternatives: Jesus Christ is the true God and eternal life
the Father is the true God and eternal life
decisions.reason: οὗτός can point to the nearest person named, Jesus Christ, or to the main subject, "the true one" of the previous sentence. For Jesus: he is the last person named; the letter calls him "the eternal life" (1:2; compare John 11:25; 14:6); and John's Gospel calls him God (John 1:1, 18; 20:28). For the Father: "the true one" has just been used of him twice; John 17:3 calls the Father "the only true God"; and the sentence would sum up that the God the Son reveals is the real God, against the idols of verse 21. Grammar alone does not decide. Every level keeps the open "this one" and the footnote gives both readings.

decisions.choice: one article over two nouns: one person who is both
decisions.reason: The article stands before "true God" only, and "eternal life" follows without its own: the same one is both the true God and eternal life.

decisions.choice: This one
decisions.reason: "He" could suggest that the subject has been settled; "this one" keeps the Greek pointer, which can refer back to either person (meaning decision m1).

records.source: Τεκνία, φυλάξατε ἑαυτὰ ἀπὸ τῶν εἰδώλων.
records.gloss: Little children, guard yourselves from the idols.
pieces: Dear children, guard yourselves against idols.

L.21: Little children, guard yourselves from the idols.

R.21: Dear children, keep away from idols, the false gods people put in the place of the true God.

decisions.choice: idols: anything put in the place of the true God, images of false gods included
alternatives: only the images worshiped in pagan temples
decisions.reason: εἴδωλον means an image of a god, and the readers lived among temples and their images. Coming straight after "the true God" (verse 20), the word sets every false god against the real one: pagan worship, and also any false picture of God, such as the teaching about Christ the letter has opposed (2:22-23; 4:1-3). The text does not narrow it.

decisions.choice: little children: a term of affection for the readers
decisions.reason: Τεκνία is the diminutive the writer uses for his readers throughout the letter (2:1, 12, 28; 3:7, 18; 4:4). It is neuter and inclusive, so the gender setting does not apply.

decisions.choice: guard yourselves: a single, decisive command
decisions.reason: The aorist imperative φυλάξατε calls for watchfulness now; the believer's guarding of himself goes with the Son's keeping in verse 18.

decisions.choice: Dear children
decisions.reason: The diminutive expresses affection (meaning decision m2); "little children" can sound as if the readers were small children. Literal keeps the diminutive.

decisions.choice: the false gods people put in the place of the true God
decisions.reason: Readable explains what an idol is and links it to verse 20 (meaning decision m1). It is an explanation of the word, not an application.
